config.title: Build request logging middleware

intro.title: Build request logging middleware
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a request logging middleware for a Node.js server. You will learn how to intercept incoming HTTP requests, log details like the request method and URL, and pass control to the next handler. The core concept is middleware—a function that processes requests in a pipeline. You'll use Node.js's built-in HTTP module and basic JavaScript functions. By the end, you'll have a working logger that outputs request information to the console.
intro.usecase: Request logging middleware is essential for monitoring and debugging production Node.js applications. In e-commerce platforms like Shopify or payment systems like Stripe, every API request is logged to track user activity, detect suspicious patterns, and troubleshoot errors. This pattern appears in admin dashboards where developers view request metrics, in security audit logs that record access attempts, and in error reporting panels that help teams identify and fix issues quickly. Implementing this middleware gives you visibility into how your application behaves in real-world scenarios.

objectives: Construct a basic middleware function that logs incoming HTTP requests
Integrate the logging middleware into an Express application
Manipulate request and response objects to extract relevant logging data
Configure middleware to execute at specific points in the request-response cycle
Apply formatting to log output for improved readability
Initialize a custom logging function with configurable options
Control the flow of execution by calling the next middleware in the chain

steps.hint: Use the require() function to import Node.js core modules. Place these imports at the top of your file.

steps.hint: Remember that middleware functions in Express/Node.js typically follow this signature: function(req, res, next) { ... }

steps.title: Define log file path
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger middleware function, create a variable named 'logFilePath' that points to 'logs/requests.log' using path.join() with __dirname.
steps.hint: Use path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log') to create the full file path.

// Example: creating a file path variable
const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'data', 'output.txt');
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware function now contains a 'logFilePath' variable that stores the full path to the log file.
successCriteria: A 'logFilePath' variable is defined inside the requestLogger function using path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using path.join() with __dirname and the correct folder structure ('logs/requests.log').
steps.feedbackWrong: The log file path wasn't defined correctly. Remember to use path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log') inside your middleware function.

steps.title: Create logs directory if it doesn't exist
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger function, use fs.existsSync() to check if the logs directory exists, and create it with fs.mkdirSync() if it doesn't.
steps.hint: First check if the directory exists, then create it only if it doesn't exist. You'll need to use the path you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware function will now ensure the logs directory exists before attempting to write log files.
successCriteria: The requestLogger function contains code that checks for the logs directory existence and creates it if missing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if the directory exists and creating it only when it doesn't. Check your logic carefully.
steps.feedbackWrong: The directory check and creation logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to use fs.existsSync() to check and fs.mkdirSync() to create the directory if it doesn't exist.

steps.title: Format the log message
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger function, create a formatted log message string that includes the current timestamp, request method, and request URL.
steps.hint: Use a template literal to combine the timestamp, method, and URL into a single string with clear formatting.

const message = `${timestamp} - ${method} ${url}`;
steps.expectedOutcome: A formatted log message string is created inside the middleware function.
successCriteria: A log message string is created that includes timestamp, method, and URL with proper formatting.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your log message includes the timestamp, method, and URL in a single formatted string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The log message formatting isn't quite right. You need to create a string that combines the timestamp, method, and URL values.

steps.title: Handle file write errors
steps.instruction: Add error handling to the fs.appendFile() call inside your requestLogger function. Use a callback function to check for errors and log them to the console if they occur.
steps.hint: The fs.appendFile() method accepts a callback function as its last parameter. This callback receives an error argument that you can check.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs.appendFile() call now includes error handling that logs any file write errors to the console.
successCriteria: The fs.appendFile() callback checks for errors and logs them to console when they occur
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking the error parameter in the callback and logging it to the console when an error occurs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handling isn't quite right. Remember that fs.appendFile() takes a callback function that receives an error parameter. Check if that error exists and log it.
